Formosa. The name means beautiful island in Portuguese, and European traders gave it to the island off the southeast coast of mainland China beginning with Portuguese contact in the sixteenth century. The indigenous name Taiwan, meaning terraced bay in Austronesian languages, gradually displaced the colonial term, especially after the island became the seat of the Republic of China in nineteen-forty-nine following the Chinese Civil War. Taiwan is now the standard English name, reflecting both indigenous heritage and the modern nation's distinct political identity from mainland China.

Portuguese explorers named the island Formosa in the sixteenth century, and the term became standard in European trade and cartography for centuries. Taiwan was inhabited by indigenous Austronesian peoples long before European contact, and the name Taiwan derives from their languages. The Dutch and Spanish colonized parts of the island in the seventeenth century, followed by the Qing Dynasty from sixteen-eighty-three to eighteen-ninety-five, when mainland Chinese control extended over it. Japan then occupied Taiwan for fifty years from eighteen-ninety-five to nineteen-forty-five after defeating China in the First Sino-Japanese War, during which time Japan developed the island's infrastructure and agriculture.

After Japan's defeat in nineteen-forty-five, the Republic of China government, the Nationalists or Kuomintang, fled the mainland and established their capital on Taiwan following the Communist victory in nineteen-forty-nine. The name Taiwan became standard internationally in the late twentieth century as the island's political identity diverged from mainland China. The shift from Formosa to Taiwan reflects not just a change in nomenclature, but the island's journey from Portuguese trade route to Japanese colony to the complex and independent society it is today.
